reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard haematology references
clinicalPearls: The most common acute hepatic porphyria; arises from partial deficiency of hydroxymethylbilane synthase (porphobilinogen deaminase) in the haem biosynthetic pathway
Attacks are dominated by severe, poorly localised abdominal pain that is often out of proportion to abdominal examination findings, with little or no peritonism
Autonomic disturbance is common, producing tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, constipation, nausea and vomiting during an attack
Neuropsychiatric features include peripheral (predominantly motor) neuropathy, confusion, anxiety, seizures and, in severe cases, respiratory muscle weakness
Hyponatraemia, frequently from SIADH, is a characteristic biochemical accompaniment and can itself provoke seizures
Attacks are precipitated by porphyrinogenic drugs, fasting or crash dieting, alcohol, infection, and cyclical hormonal changes; the majority of gene carriers remain clinically latent
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating markedly raised urinary porphobilinogen and delta-aminolaevulinic acid during an attack; freshly voided urine may darken on standing

Management principles are removal of precipitants, high carbohydrate intake, and intravenous haem (haem arginate) to downregulate ALA synthase, alongside symptom control and monitoring for respiratory or bulbar compromise
Skin is not photosensitive in AIP, distinguishing it from the cutaneous porphyrias
reference.pathophysiology: Acute intermittent porphyria results from an autosomal dominant, partial deficiency of hydroxymethylbilane synthase, the third enzyme of haem biosynthesis. Reduced enzyme activity alone does not cause symptoms, but when hepatic haem demand rises, ALA synthase (the rate-limiting first enzyme) is induced and the pathway bottleneck causes accumulation of the porphyrin precursors delta-aminolaevulinic acid (ALA) and porphobilinogen (PBG). These precursors, particularly ALA, are thought to be neurotoxic and underlie the autonomic, peripheral and central neurological manifestations. Many drugs, hormones, fasting and stress induce hepatic ALA synthase, explaining why attacks are precipitated by these factors.
additionalDifferentials: Surgical acute abdomen (appendicitis, bowel obstruction, perforation)
Lead poisoning (also raises ALA and can mimic acute porphyria)
Other acute hepatic porphyrias (variegate porphyria, hereditary coproporphyria)
Guillain-Barre syndrome and other acute neuropathies
Primary psychiatric illness or functional abdominal pain
additionalInvestigations: Urinary porphobilinogen and delta-aminolaevulinic acid during a symptomatic episode
Quantitative urinary, faecal and plasma porphyrin profiling to distinguish porphyria subtypes
Serum sodium and osmolality to detect hyponatraemia and SIADH
Erythrocyte hydroxymethylbilane synthase activity and molecular genetic testing for confirmation and family screening
Blood lead level to exclude lead poisoning as a mimic
redFlags: Acute attack with progressive motor weakness or respiratory muscle involvement threatening ventilatory failure
Severe hyponatraemia or seizures during an attack
Bulbar dysfunction with risk of aspiration
Continued exposure to a porphyrinogenic drug or precipitant during an ongoing attack
Severe autonomic instability with labile blood pressure and arrhythmia
reference.prognosis: With prompt recognition, removal of precipitants and haem therapy most acute attacks resolve, though recovery from established motor neuropathy can be slow and incomplete. Recurrent attacks and long-term complications such as chronic hypertension, renal impairment and an increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma may occur, and untreated severe attacks can be fatal from respiratory failure or arrhythmia.
pitfalls: Attributing severe abdominal pain to a surgical cause and proceeding to unnecessary laparotomy
Giving porphyrinogenic drugs (many anticonvulsants, sulfonamides and others) that worsen or trigger an attack
Missing the diagnosis because skin findings are absent
Failing to check a symptomatic urine sample for porphobilinogen before treatment alters results
Overlooking hyponatraemia and its role in seizures
